newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's army braces for Palestinian anger.
newsitem.headline: Israel's army braces for Palestinian anger.

text.p: Israeli troops commanding overwhelming firepower are braced to face angry Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip following a Washington summit which Israel has hailed a victory but the PLO has called a failure.
"The results of the summit are a great success from the point of view of the government of Israel," Israeli cabinet secretary Danny Naveh told Israel Radio from Washington after the Wednesday talks.
"The summit has failed because of Israeli intransigence," Hasan Asfour, a Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) negotiator, told Reuters.
While Palestinians were united in disappointment, Israelis were divided over what their government termed a victory.

"I think that Bibi Netanyahu gambled in Washington with the fate of the state," Yossi Sarid, member of parliament and head of the leftist Meretz party, told Israel's army radio, using Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's nickname.
"No one can know right now how many people will have to pay with their lives for this wild gamble," he said.

Pinchas Wallerstein, leader of some 130,000 Jews settled amid the nearly two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, told Reuters: "I'm very glad about the prime minister's firm position but on the other hand I'm worried about the Palestinian reaction."
In the West Bank on Wednesday, Israeli troops, enforcing sweeping restrictions on movement in the areas, killed one Arab and wounded five, the Israeli army and Palestinians said.

It raised the death toll to 58 Palestinians and 15 Israelis since last week when Israel's opening of a second entrance to a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem sparked widespread gun battles and clashes.

Israeli television said the Jewish state's army, which has ringed Palestinian self-rule enclaves with tanks, was ready for the "worst case scenario". Israel Radio said most training of troops had stopped as they reinforced the West Bank and Gaza.

Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, touring Jewish settlements in the Gaza Strip before the summit ended, told reporters: "We will not allow them to open fire at our soldiers ...We will act with all the severity demanded."

President Bill Clinton on Wednesday told a White House news conference after the two-day summit that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Netanyahu failed to resolve their differences. He said the Middle East peace process was still in crisis.
"The peace process is on the verge of collapse," said Mustafa Natsheh, Palestinian mayor of Hebron on the West Bank, a town that is a major point of contention between the sides.
"Unless international and Arab public opinion and Israeli peace groups move, the area will not witness any calm and the cycle of violence will return anew," he said.
Arafat had demanded Netanyahu carry out an Israeli troop redeployment in Hebron as agreed in a signed deal with Israel's previous centre-left government as well as close the tunnel.
Clinton said the two sides had agreed to resume immediate peace talks focusing on an Israeli pullback from Hebron, far less than Arafat's demand for the immediate redeployment.

Faisal al-Husseini, senior PLO representative in Jerusalem, told Israel Radio: "In this situation tomorrow there is a possibility that there will be nothing but there is a possibility that there will be another explosion."
He added: "I was never as pessimistic as I am today."
